subject.title: What Will You Do?
subject.author: Rainer Maria Rilke
subject.text:
By Rainer Maria Rilke
What will you do, God, when I die?
I am your jar (if cracked, I lie?)
Your well-spring (if the well go dry?)
I am your craft, your vesture I-
You lose your purport, losing me.

When I go, your cold house will be
Empty of words that made it sweet.
I am the sandals your bare feet
Will seek and long for, wearily.
Your cloak will fall from aching bones.
Your glance, that my warm cheeks have cheered
As with a cushion long endeared,
Will wonder at a loss so weird;
And, when the sun has disappeared,
Lie in the lap of alien stones.
What will you do, God? I am feared.

             AN OLD WOMAN PASSES
                                 By Franz Werfel

title: The Prayer That Leaves God Homeless
standfirst: Written in twenty-five days after a trip to Russia, this 1899 prayer is spoken by a monk Rilke invented, addressed to a God who cannot survive without him. Its English translators, working not two years into a marriage that would run for decades, gave it a pun the German never made.

sections.heading: The Usual Arithmetic, Reversed
sections.body:
A prayer usually runs one way: the small, mortal party asks the large, permanent one to keep existing. Rilke's monk runs the sum backwards. He lists what he is to God — a jar, a well-spring, a craftsman's trade, a garment — and attaches a small catastrophe in parentheses to each one, as if talking himself into the fear even as he states it.

> I am your jar (if cracked, I lie?)
> Your well-spring (if the well go dry?)
> I am your craft, your vesture I—
> You lose your purport, losing me.

Break the vessel and the meaning it carried breaks too. By the poem's own logic, God is the dependent one here, and the man saying the prayer holds the upper hand. He does not sound like it. He sounds afraid.

sections.heading: Twenty-Five Days in Schmargendorf
sections.body:
Rilke wrote the whole of *Das Buch vom mönchischen Leben* — the book this prayer belongs to — between the 20th of September and the 14th of October 1899, working in Berlin-Schmargendorf. He was twenty-three. He had just come back from his first trip to Russia, made that spring and early summer with Lou Andreas-Salomé, and the book arrived as a kind of overflow from it: a sequence originally called simply *Die Gebete* — The Prayers — and dedicated, in his own words on the manuscript, "gelegt in die Hände von Lou": placed in Lou's hands.

That speed matters. This is not a poem revised over years into its argument. It is one of roughly a hundred that came out of Rilke in under a month, the God-needs-me conceit arrived at and set down while the trip that produced it was still fresh enough to argue with.

sections.heading: A Russian Monk Who Never Existed
sections.body:
The voice saying all this is invented. Rilke gives the poem to a fictional Russian icon-painter monk, a persona built out of what the 1899 trip had shown him: villages where, as he later described it, Orthodox peasant devotion was total and unembarrassed, and meetings with the painter Leonid Pasternak and with Tolstoy himself. The Russian iconostasis — the wall of painted panels that stands between a congregation and its altar, mediating rather than explaining — gave him a working model for a God encountered at close range, through objects, rather than argued about from a pulpit.

It is a borrowed voice for a private theology. Rilke was not Orthodox, was barely churchgoing at all, but the monk let him say things about need and dependency that a poem signed in his own name might have had to qualify.

sections.heading: A Pun the German Never Made
sections.body:
Set the translation the sheet above shows you against Rilke's own German and one line stops matching:

> Ich bin dein Krug (wenn ich zerscherbe?)

*Krug* is jar or pitcher; *zerscherbe* is to shatter into shards. There is no wordplay in it — just a vessel breaking. Babette Deutsch and Avrahm Yarmolinsky's English adds one: "I am your jar (if cracked, I lie?)", where *lie* can mean lying in pieces on the floor or telling an untruth, and a cracked jar might plausibly do either. It is a good pun. It is also theirs, not Rilke's — a translator's decision to trade a small fidelity for a better English line.

The closing line takes a different kind of liberty. Rilke's monk ends "Ich bin bange" — literally, I am afraid. Deutsch and Yarmolinsky render it "I am feared," which asks the same German words to describe something closer to being frightening than to being frightened. Whether that is a slip or a deliberate ambiguity — a man discovering that his own necessity makes him formidable — the sheet gives you both texts to decide for yourself.

sections.heading: Not Two Years Married
sections.body:
Deutsch and Yarmolinsky had married on the 28th of April 1921 — she a Barnard graduate and working poet, he the newly appointed head of the New York Public Library's Slavonic Division. That same year the two of them published *Modern Russian Poetry: An Anthology* together. This Rilke translation ran in *Poetry* magazine in December 1922, not two years into the marriage, and it was headed for a second collection: *Contemporary German Poetry: An Anthology*, which they brought out in 1923.

It reads, in other words, as apprentice work from a partnership just getting up to speed — one that would go on translating together for the next five decades, including a full English *Eugene Onegin*, while Yarmolinsky ran the Slavonic Division for thirty-seven years and Deutsch went on to teach at Columbia.

sections.heading: Sixty Thousand Copies of a Prayer
sections.body:
Rilke sat on the manuscript for six years before he would let it out. *Das Stunden-Buch* — the finished book, this monastic sequence plus two later ones written the same way in later years — did not reach print until December 1905, and only then as his first book for Insel Verlag, the publisher that would carry the rest of his career. It sold. Four editions and roughly sixty thousand copies went out in his lifetime, an improbable number for a sequence of prayers spoken by an invented Russian monk.

The translator Edward Snow later called it "one of the strongest inaugural works in all of modern poetry. It arrives as if out of nowhere and seems to want to wipe the slate clean." The poem on the sheet above is where that clean slate starts: a monk telling his God, in effect, that the debt runs the other way.
